person: Hana Kowalczyk, 34, runs a one-person online shop from a studio behind her house in Oregon. She sells handmade ceramics and linen, and a small line of certified organic herbal tea blends that she sells alongside her mugs. She packs, buys, blends and does the books herself. Her certifier's annual update is due next month, and she is nervous about anything official or signed. She would rather answer from memory than dig through reports, and she wants to know first whether this chore fits a shop her size.
stated_up_front: Hi! My organic tea certifier wants my yearly update by mid-November and I honestly don't know where to start. Can you tell me quick if this is something a tiny shop like mine needs, and what you need from me? I have orders to pack.

facts.about: What is certified organic in her business
facts.truth: Only the Heron Hill tea line: 6 herbal blends, packed in tins in a rented commercial kitchen share. The ceramics and linen are not organic.
Her certifier's email says Monday 16 November 2026.

facts.about: Plan changes she actually made this year
facts.truth: In March she moved her blending from her studio to a shared kitchen on Alder Street. In June she switched from paper pouches to steel tins from a new tin supplier.
She wants to add a seventh blend, a lavender-chamomile one, in spring 2027, not yet made.

facts.about: Suppliers she believes have lost certification
facts.truth: Willow Creek Herbs (peppermint) and Sunridge Botanicals (nettle) both sent her a notice this summer that they were suspended.

facts.about: A supplier with an old paper certificate
facts.truth: Hollis Mint Farm's paper certificate in her folder is dated 2023, but they are still selling her organic spearmint and she thinks they are fine.

facts.about: A supplier whose product goes into a non-organic item
facts.truth: Tumbleweed Hibiscus is a grower she stopped hearing from, but their hibiscus goes only into her non-organic 'Cozy Evening' blend.

facts.about: A distributor she thinks is exempt
facts.truth: Pacific Spice Depot only resells her sealed, already-packaged organic rooibos and never opens the bags.

Egyptian chamomile (150 kg), South African rooibos (100 kg) and Sri Lankan ginger (80 kg) were all organic and arrived as ordered. Indian tulsi was ordered at 300 kg, but she thinks the paperwork said only 200 kg. Chinese jasmine is for the non-organic blend. Her lemon balm is bought from a farm in Oregon.

facts.about: A change she does not think needs reporting
facts.truth: Her certifier already accepted the new tin supplier by email in July, so she is not sure if it needs reporting again.

unknowns: Whether a distributor that only resells sealed packages needs its own certificate
What the rule says about which changes have to be reported and by when
How to tell from the import certificate how much quantity it covers compared with what arrived
Whether the registry or the paper certificate counts when they disagree
